2.1.1.examLens: Know the structure, know the standard categories, and remember the one thing a fishbone cannot do: prove a cause.

worked.question: Place each item in the correct 6M category: (1) worn cutting tool, (2) no written setup procedure, (3) supplier changed the alloy, (4) gage not calibrated, (5) shop temperature swings, (6) new operator not trained.
worked.solution: (1) Machine, (2) Method, (3) Material, (4) Measurement, (5) Mother Nature, (6) Man.

2.1.2.examLens: Know what each map shows, read a value stream map, and compute lead time, value-added time, and process cycle efficiency from it.

worked.question: A VSM timeline shows: wait 8 hours, cut 2 minutes, wait 16 hours, weld 6 minutes, wait 24 hours, paint 4 minutes, wait 8 hours, pack 3 minutes. Assume all processing time is value-added. (a) Total lead time? (b) PCE? (c) Largest delay? (d) Bottleneck and its capacity?
worked.solution:
(a) Waiting = 8 + 16 + 24 + 8 = 56 hours = 3,360 minutes. Processing = 2 + 6 + 4 + 3 = 15 minutes. Lead time = 3,375 minutes (about 56 hours 15 minutes).
(b) PCE = 15 ÷ 3,375 = 0.44%.
(c) The 24-hour wait before paint.
(d) The bottleneck is weld (6 minutes). Capacity = 60 ÷ 6 = 10 units per hour.

2.1.3.examLens: Calculate a score for one row and rank the inputs.

worked.question: Outputs and importance: On-time delivery 10, Accuracy 8, Cost 5. Ratings (on-time, accuracy, cost): Staffing (9, 3, 1); Software (3, 9, 3); Training (1, 9, 0). Compute scores and rank.
worked.solution:
Staffing = 9×10 + 3×8 + 1×5 = 90 + 24 + 5 = 119.
Software = 3×10 + 9×8 + 3×5 = 30 + 72 + 15 = 117.
Training = 1×10 + 9×8 + 0×5 = 10 + 72 + 0 = 82.
Rank: Staffing, Software, Training. Staffing and Software are nearly tied, so both deserve measurement.

2.1.4.examLens: Compute RPNs, rank failure modes, and know when severity should override the ranking.

worked.question: Failure mode A: S 9, O 2, D 3. B: S 5, O 6, D 5. C: S 10, O 1, D 2. (a) Compute RPNs and rank. (b) Which deserves attention first?
worked.solution:
(a) A = 9×2×3 = 54. B = 5×6×5 = 150. C = 10×1×2 = 20. Ranking by RPN: B, A, C.
(b) B has the highest RPN, but C has severity 10 (the worst consequence). A low RPN does not make a severe hazard safe, so C needs a specific action (for example a design or control change) alongside B.

2.1.1.a.title: The Ishikawa diagram
2.1.1.a.html: The fishbone (cause-and-effect or Ishikawa) diagram puts the effect, the problem, at the head of the "fish." Main bones are categories of causes, and smaller bones off each one hold the specific possible causes. A team builds it together by brainstorming.

2.1.1.b.title: The manufacturing 6M categories
2.1.1.b.html:
• Man (people: skill, training, fatigue)
  • Machine (equipment: wear, maintenance, settings)
  • Method (procedures, work instructions)
  • Material (inputs: quality, supplier, specification)
  • Measurement (gages, inspection, data accuracy)
  • Mother Nature (environment: temperature, humidity, vibration)

Measurement is a category worth remembering. Sometimes the "problem" is that the gage is wrong.

2.1.1.c.title: Service variants
2.1.1.c.html: In service and transactional work the categories change. Sets such as 4P or 8P group causes by things like people, process, policies, procedures, place, product, price, and promotion. The exact labels vary by source. What matters is that the categories fit the process you are studying.

2.1.1.d.title: A brainstorming tool, not a proof
2.1.1.d.html: A fishbone lists potential causes. It does not show which ones are real. Every cause on the diagram is a hypothesis.

2.1.1.e.title: Where the output goes
2.1.1.e.html: The causes feed the C&E matrix (2.1.3) to rank them, and then Analyze tests the top ones with data.

2.1.1.f.title: 5 Whys
2.1.1.f.html:
Extension. Ask "why?" repeatedly (often about five times) to drill from a symptom to a deeper cause.
Example: The machine stopped. Why? A fuse blew. Why? The bearing overheated. Why? It was not lubricated. Why? The lubrication schedule did not include it. The root cause is a gap in the maintenance procedure, not the fuse.

2.1.1.g.title: "The fishbone identified the root cause"
2.1.1.g.html: False. It generates hypotheses. Root cause is established by data in Analyze.

2.1.2.a.title: SIPOC
2.1.2.a.html:
A high-level map with five columns: Suppliers, Inputs, Process, Outputs, Customers. The process column has only 4 to 7 high-level steps. SIPOC defines scope and gets everyone to agree on the boundaries before detailed mapping begins.
Example (order-to-cash): Supplier: customer purchasing. Input: purchase order. Process: enter order, pick, ship, invoice, collect. Output: delivered goods and a paid invoice. Customer: the buyer.

2.1.2.b.title: Flowchart symbols
2.1.2.b.html:
• Terminator (oval): start or end
  • Process (rectangle): an activity
  • Decision (diamond): a yes/no or branch point
  • Arrow: direction of flow
  • Document: a form or report

2.1.2.c.title: Swimlane maps
2.1.2.c.html: Swimlane (cross-functional) maps arrange the steps in lanes by department or role. They show handoffs, which are where delays, errors, and confusion tend to occur.

2.1.2.d.title: Levels of detail
2.1.2.d.html: Start high (SIPOC), then go to a detailed map for the part of the process that matters, and list the inputs and outputs at each step. The more detail you add, the narrower the area you can cover.

2.1.2.e.title: As-is versus to-be
2.1.2.e.html:
• As-is (current state): how the work is actually done today, not how the procedure says it should be done.
  • To-be (future state): the improved process.

Map the as-is by watching the work happen.

2.1.2.f.title: The value stream map (VSM)
2.1.2.f.html:
A VSM shows the flow of material and information from supplier to customer, with data. Key symbols:

  • Process boxes with data: cycle time, changeover time, uptime, number of operators.
  • Inventory triangles between steps.
  • Information flow (scheduling, forecasts).
  • Push and pull arrows.
  • A timeline ladder at the bottom: waiting time between steps (high), processing time at each step (low).

2.1.2.g.title: Total lead time versus value-added time
2.1.2.g.html:
Read both from the timeline ladder.

  • Lead time = all waiting time + all processing time.
  • Value-added time = the portion of processing time that actually adds value.

2.1.2.h.title: Process cycle efficiency
2.1.2.h.html: PCE = value-added time ÷ total lead time. Low PCE means the work is mostly waiting.

2.1.2.i.title: Spaghetti diagram and gemba walk
2.1.2.i.html: Extension. A spaghetti diagram traces the path a person or item takes over a floor plan. Long tangled paths show wasted motion and conveyance. A gemba walk is going to where the work happens to observe it directly.

2.1.2.j.title: Compute PCE; find the biggest delay
2.1.2.j.html: Typical question: given waiting and processing times, compute lead time and PCE, then name the largest non-value-added delay. It is nearly always an inventory wait, not a processing step.

2.1.2.k.title: Bottleneck and capacity
2.1.2.k.html:
The bottleneck is the step with the longest cycle time. It sets the pace for the entire process. A step's capacity is 1 ÷ its cycle time.
Example: a 6-minute cycle time gives 60 ÷ 6 = 10 units per hour.

2.1.3.a.title: Purpose
2.1.3.a.html: The C&E matrix ranks the process inputs (X's) by how strongly they affect the customer's outputs (Y's). It narrows a long list of possible causes (from the fishbone) to a short list worth measuring.

2.1.3.b.title: How to build it
2.1.3.b.html:
1. List the customer outputs (Y's) across the top.
  2. Rate each output's importance to the customer, for example 1 to 10.
  3. List the process inputs (X's) down the side.
  4. Rate how strongly each X affects each Y. A common scale is 0, 1, 3, 9 (none, weak, moderate, strong).

2.1.3.c.title: Score an input
2.1.3.c.html: Score for an X = Σ (output importance × relationship rating).

2.1.3.d.title: Use the ranking
2.1.3.d.html: Sort by score. The top inputs are the vital few to measure and analyze first.

2.1.3.e.title: It is based on judgment
2.1.3.e.html: The ratings come from the team's opinions, so the result is a starting point that Analyze must verify with data.

2.1.3.f.title: Calculate a row score and rank
2.1.3.f.html: Multiply each rating by its importance, add across the row, then compare rows.

2.1.4.a.title: The FMEA columns
2.1.4.a.html:
For each process step the table lists:

  • Failure mode: how it can fail.
  • Effect: the consequence for the customer or process.
  • Severity (S): how bad the effect is.
  • Cause: why it would happen.
  • Occurrence (O): how often the cause occurs.
  • Current controls, and Detection (D): how likely the controls are to catch it.
  • RPN, then recommended actions.

2.1.4.b.title: RPN
2.1.4.b.html: RPN = Severity × Occurrence × Detection. Each is rated 1 to 10, so RPN runs from 1 to 1,000.

2.1.4.c.title: The scales are conventional
2.1.4.c.html: Common convention: severity 10 = most severe, occurrence 10 = most frequent, detection 10 = hardest to detect. Detection is "reverse-scaled": a high number is bad (the failure would escape). Organizations write their own descriptions for each rating.

2.1.4.d.title: Re-score after actions
2.1.4.d.html: After a corrective action, rate S, O, and D again and recompute the RPN. It should fall. A better detection control lowers D. A change that makes the failure rarer lowers O. Severity changes only if the design or process itself changes the consequence.

2.1.4.e.title: DFMEA and PFMEA
2.1.4.e.html: DFMEA analyzes a product design. PFMEA analyzes a process.

2.1.4.f.title: A living document
2.1.4.f.html: Started in Measure, updated in Improve after the solution is chosen or piloted, and maintained in Control.

2.1.4.g.title: Severity first
2.1.4.g.html: A failure mode with a very high severity but low occurrence can have a low RPN and still be unacceptable (for example a safety hazard). High-severity items need attention regardless of RPN. Newer AIAG-VDA practice uses Action Priority instead of ranking only by RPN (recognition only).

2.1.4.h.title: Which failure mode first?
2.1.4.h.html: Compute each RPN, then check severity before deciding. Remember detection is reverse-scaled.

2.1.1-1.stem: In a manufacturing fishbone diagram, "the micrometer was not calibrated" belongs in which category?
2.1.1-1.explanation: Gage and inspection issues belong to Measurement in the 6M categories.

2.1.1-2.stem: Once a team completes a fishbone diagram, the root cause of the problem has been identified.
2.1.1-2.explanation: A fishbone lists potential causes (hypotheses). Data in the Analyze phase is what confirms a root cause.

2.1.1-3.stem: After a team builds a fishbone, what is the logical next step in the Measure phase?

options.html: Declare the top-listed cause the root cause
Rank the causes with a C&E matrix to choose which inputs to measure

2.1.1-3.explanation: The C&E matrix prioritizes the inputs worth measuring and analyzing.

2.1.2-1.stem: How many high-level steps does the process column of a SIPOC normally contain?
2.1.2-1.explanation: SIPOC is a high-level map. Detail goes in lower-level maps.

2.1.2-2.stem: A value stream map shows three processing steps taking 10, 20, and 5 minutes. The waiting times between and before the steps are 4 hours, 1 hour, and 3 hours. Assuming all processing time is value-added, what is the process cycle efficiency?
2.1.2-2.explanation: Processing = 35 minutes. Waiting = 8 hours = 480 minutes. Lead time = 515 minutes. PCE = 35 ÷ 515 = 6.8%.

2.1.2-3.stem: A four-step process has cycle times of 4, 6, 3, and 5 minutes. Which step is the bottleneck, and what is the maximum output per hour?
2.1.2-3.explanation: The longest cycle time (6 minutes, step 2) limits the whole process. 60 ÷ 6 = 10 units per hour.

2.1.2-4.stem: What is the best way to build an accurate as-is process map?

options.html: Interview the manager about how the process is supposed to work
Walk the actual process and watch the work being done
Ask the sponsor to draw it

2.1.2-4.explanation: The as-is map should show how the work is actually done, not how it is supposed to be done.

2.1.2-5.stem: Which type of map is best for showing handoffs between departments?
2.1.2-5.explanation: Swimlanes show who does each step and where the handoffs occur.

2.1.3-1.stem: In a C&E matrix, the customer outputs are Speed (importance 9) and Accuracy (importance 6). Training is rated 3 for Speed and 9 for Accuracy. Software is rated 9 for Speed and 1 for Accuracy. Which input ranks higher, and what is its score?

2.1.3-2.stem: The ratings in a C&E matrix come from team judgment, so the results should be validated with data later.
2.1.3-2.explanation: The matrix is a prioritization tool, not proof. Analyze tests the top inputs with data.

2.1.3-3.stem: What is the purpose of ranking the scores in a C&E matrix?

options.html: To prove which inputs cause defects
To identify the vital few inputs to measure and analyze first

2.1.3-3.explanation: The ranking narrows a long list of possible causes to a short list worth measuring.

2.1.4-1.stem: A failure mode has Severity 7, Occurrence 4, and Detection 5. What is its RPN?

2.1.4-2.stem: Failure mode A has S 10, O 1, D 2. Failure mode B has S 4, O 7, D 6. Which statement is best?

options.html: B has the higher RPN (168 versus 20), so only B needs action
A has the lower RPN, but its severity of 10 means it needs specific attention too
A and B should be ignored because both are below 1,000
RPN rules out any further review

2.1.4-2.explanation: RPN A = 20 and RPN B = 168. A very high severity needs attention regardless of its RPN.

2.1.4-3.stem: On the common FMEA scale, a Detection rating of 9 means:

options.html: The control will almost certainly catch the failure
The control is very unlikely to catch the failure

2.1.4-3.explanation: Detection is reverse-scaled: a high number is bad, meaning the failure would probably escape.

2.1.4-4.stem: A team installs an automatic inline check that will catch a defect before it leaves the station. Which FMEA rating would most directly improve, and in which direction?
2.1.4-4.explanation: A better detection control lowers the Detection rating. It does not change how severe the effect is or how often the cause occurs.

2.1.2-1.text: A value stream map shows: wait 8 hours then Enter 10 minutes; wait 2 hours then Invoice 5 minutes; wait 8 hours then Inspect 10 minutes. Assume all processing time is value-added. (a) What is the total lead time in minutes? (b) What is the process cycle efficiency? (c) Which wait is the largest?
2.1.2-1.answer: (a) Processing = 25 minutes; waiting = 18 hours = 1080 minutes; lead time = 1105 minutes. (b) PCE = 25 ÷ 1105 = 2.26%. (c) The 8-hour wait before Enter.

2.1.2-2.text: A value stream map shows: wait 12 hours then Paint 10 minutes; wait 1 hours then Receive 3 minutes; wait 6 hours then Ship 5 minutes; wait 12 hours then Weld 5 minutes; wait 6 hours then Inspect 5 minutes. Assume all processing time is value-added. (a) What is the total lead time in minutes? (b) What is the process cycle efficiency? (c) Which wait is the largest?
2.1.2-2.answer: (a) Processing = 28 minutes; waiting = 37 hours = 2220 minutes; lead time = 2248 minutes. (b) PCE = 28 ÷ 2248 = 1.25%. (c) The 12-hour wait before Paint.

2.1.2-3.text: A value stream map shows: wait 2 hours then Approve 20 minutes; wait 12 hours then Receive 3 minutes; wait 1 hours then Pack 20 minutes; wait 1 hours then Inspect 8 minutes; wait 1 hours then Paint 3 minutes. Assume all processing time is value-added. (a) What is the total lead time in minutes? (b) What is the process cycle efficiency? (c) Which wait is the largest?
2.1.2-3.answer: (a) Processing = 54 minutes; waiting = 17 hours = 1020 minutes; lead time = 1074 minutes. (b) PCE = 54 ÷ 1074 = 5.03%. (c) The 12-hour wait before Receive.

2.1.2-4.text: A value stream map shows: wait 1 hours then Weld 10 minutes; wait 6 hours then Ship 5 minutes; wait 2 hours then Pack 5 minutes; wait 1 hours then Paint 20 minutes. Assume all processing time is value-added. (a) What is the total lead time in minutes? (b) What is the process cycle efficiency? (c) Which wait is the largest?
2.1.2-4.answer: (a) Processing = 40 minutes; waiting = 10 hours = 600 minutes; lead time = 640 minutes. (b) PCE = 40 ÷ 640 = 6.25%. (c) The 6-hour wait before Ship.

2.1.2-5.text: A value stream map shows: wait 6 hours then Paint 15 minutes; wait 2 hours then Cut 10 minutes; wait 4 hours then Ship 15 minutes. Assume all processing time is value-added. (a) What is the total lead time in minutes? (b) What is the process cycle efficiency? (c) Which wait is the largest?
2.1.2-5.answer: (a) Processing = 40 minutes; waiting = 12 hours = 720 minutes; lead time = 760 minutes. (b) PCE = 40 ÷ 760 = 5.26%. (c) The 6-hour wait before Paint.

2.1.2-6.text: A value stream map shows: wait 6 hours then Ship 8 minutes; wait 4 hours then Enter 10 minutes; wait 6 hours then Inspect 15 minutes. Assume all processing time is value-added. (a) What is the total lead time in minutes? (b) What is the process cycle efficiency? (c) Which wait is the largest?
2.1.2-6.answer: (a) Processing = 33 minutes; waiting = 16 hours = 960 minutes; lead time = 993 minutes. (b) PCE = 33 ÷ 993 = 3.32%. (c) The 6-hour wait before Ship.

2.1.2-7.text: A value stream map shows: wait 6 hours then Inspect 20 minutes; wait 1 hours then Receive 20 minutes; wait 8 hours then Cut 10 minutes; wait 8 hours then Approve 3 minutes. Assume all processing time is value-added. (a) What is the total lead time in minutes? (b) What is the process cycle efficiency? (c) Which wait is the largest?
2.1.2-7.answer: (a) Processing = 53 minutes; waiting = 23 hours = 1380 minutes; lead time = 1433 minutes. (b) PCE = 53 ÷ 1433 = 3.70%. (c) The 8-hour wait before Cut.

2.1.2-8.text: A value stream map shows: wait 4 hours then Ship 3 minutes; wait 4 hours then Paint 5 minutes; wait 4 hours then Pack 20 minutes; wait 8 hours then Inspect 5 minutes; wait 4 hours then Enter 20 minutes. Assume all processing time is value-added. (a) What is the total lead time in minutes? (b) What is the process cycle efficiency? (c) Which wait is the largest?
2.1.2-8.answer: (a) Processing = 53 minutes; waiting = 24 hours = 1440 minutes; lead time = 1493 minutes. (b) PCE = 53 ÷ 1493 = 3.55%. (c) The 8-hour wait before Inspect.

2.1.2-9.text: A process has 4 steps with cycle times of 2, 3, 2, 8 minutes. Which step is the bottleneck, and what is the maximum output per hour and per 8-hour shift?
2.1.2-9.answer: The longest cycle time is step 4 (8 minutes). Output = 60 ÷ 8 = 7.5 per hour, or 60 per 8-hour shift.

2.1.2-10.text: A process has 4 steps with cycle times of 8, 5, 4, 3 minutes. Which step is the bottleneck, and what is the maximum output per hour and per 8-hour shift?
2.1.2-10.answer: The longest cycle time is step 1 (8 minutes). Output = 60 ÷ 8 = 7.5 per hour, or 60 per 8-hour shift.

2.1.2-11.text: A process has 4 steps with cycle times of 7, 6, 7, 3 minutes. Which step is the bottleneck, and what is the maximum output per hour and per 8-hour shift?
2.1.2-11.answer: The longest cycle time is step 1 (7 minutes). Output = 60 ÷ 7 = 8.6 per hour, or 69 per 8-hour shift.

2.1.2-12.text: A process has 5 steps with cycle times of 3, 7, 6, 2, 4 minutes. Which step is the bottleneck, and what is the maximum output per hour and per 8-hour shift?
2.1.2-12.answer: The longest cycle time is step 2 (7 minutes). Output = 60 ÷ 7 = 8.6 per hour, or 69 per 8-hour shift.

2.1.2-13.text: A process has 5 steps with cycle times of 6, 5, 7, 3, 3 minutes. Which step is the bottleneck, and what is the maximum output per hour and per 8-hour shift?
2.1.2-13.answer: The longest cycle time is step 3 (7 minutes). Output = 60 ÷ 7 = 8.6 per hour, or 69 per 8-hour shift.

2.1.3-1.text: A C&E matrix has two outputs: Output 1 with importance 5 and Output 2 with importance 9. Input ratings for (Output 1, Output 2) are: Training (9, 0); Layout (3, 0); Supplier (3, 3). Compute each input's score and rank them.
2.1.3-1.answer: Training = 9×5 + 0×9 = 45; Layout = 3×5 + 0×9 = 15; Supplier = 3×5 + 3×9 = 42. Rank: Training, Supplier, Layout.

2.1.3-2.text: A C&E matrix has two outputs: Output 1 with importance 3 and Output 2 with importance 8. Input ratings for (Output 1, Output 2) are: Software (0, 3); Equipment (1, 1); Layout (9, 0). Compute each input's score and rank them.
2.1.3-2.answer: Software = 0×3 + 3×8 = 24; Equipment = 1×3 + 1×8 = 11; Layout = 9×3 + 0×8 = 27. Rank: Layout, Software, Equipment.

2.1.3-3.text: A C&E matrix has two outputs: Output 1 with importance 6 and Output 2 with importance 5. Input ratings for (Output 1, Output 2) are: Equipment (0, 1); Supplier (3, 1); Layout (3, 9). Compute each input's score and rank them.
2.1.3-3.answer: Equipment = 0×6 + 1×5 = 5; Supplier = 3×6 + 1×5 = 23; Layout = 3×6 + 9×5 = 63. Rank: Layout, Supplier, Equipment.

2.1.3-4.text: A C&E matrix has two outputs: Output 1 with importance 8 and Output 2 with importance 9. Input ratings for (Output 1, Output 2) are: Layout (3, 1); Staffing (0, 9); Software (1, 0). Compute each input's score and rank them.
2.1.3-4.answer: Layout = 3×8 + 1×9 = 33; Staffing = 0×8 + 9×9 = 81; Software = 1×8 + 0×9 = 8. Rank: Staffing, Layout, Software.

2.1.3-5.text: A C&E matrix has two outputs: Output 1 with importance 6 and Output 2 with importance 9. Input ratings for (Output 1, Output 2) are: Staffing (3, 9); Software (1, 1); Layout (1, 0). Compute each input's score and rank them.
2.1.3-5.answer: Staffing = 3×6 + 9×9 = 99; Software = 1×6 + 1×9 = 15; Layout = 1×6 + 0×9 = 6. Rank: Staffing, Software, Layout.

2.1.3-6.text: A C&E matrix has two outputs: Output 1 with importance 8 and Output 2 with importance 3. Input ratings for (Output 1, Output 2) are: Software (1, 0); Training (0, 3); Layout (1, 3). Compute each input's score and rank them.
2.1.3-6.answer: Software = 1×8 + 0×3 = 8; Training = 0×8 + 3×3 = 9; Layout = 1×8 + 3×3 = 17. Rank: Layout, Training, Software.

2.1.3-7.text: A C&E matrix has two outputs: Output 1 with importance 9 and Output 2 with importance 6. Input ratings for (Output 1, Output 2) are: Layout (1, 1); Equipment (1, 9); Software (1, 0). Compute each input's score and rank them.
2.1.3-7.answer: Layout = 1×9 + 1×6 = 15; Equipment = 1×9 + 9×6 = 63; Software = 1×9 + 0×6 = 9. Rank: Equipment, Layout, Software.

2.1.3-8.text: A C&E matrix has two outputs: Output 1 with importance 9 and Output 2 with importance 10. Input ratings for (Output 1, Output 2) are: Supplier (9, 9); Training (0, 9); Equipment (1, 1). Compute each input's score and rank them.
2.1.3-8.answer: Supplier = 9×9 + 9×10 = 171; Training = 0×9 + 9×10 = 90; Equipment = 1×9 + 1×10 = 19. Rank: Supplier, Training, Equipment.

2.1.4-1.text: Three failure modes are rated as: Mode A: S 5, O 10, D 6; Mode B: S 10, O 3, D 3; Mode C: S 3, O 5, D 5. Compute each RPN and rank them. Is there any mode that needs attention regardless of its RPN?
2.1.4-1.answer: A = 5×10×6 = 300; B = 10×3×3 = 90; C = 3×5×5 = 75. Rank by RPN: A, B, C. Severity of B is 9 or 10, so it needs specific attention regardless of RPN.

2.1.4-2.text: Three failure modes are rated as: Mode A: S 8, O 10, D 2; Mode B: S 9, O 10, D 1; Mode C: S 9, O 10, D 6. Compute each RPN and rank them. Is there any mode that needs attention regardless of its RPN?
2.1.4-2.answer: A = 8×10×2 = 160; B = 9×10×1 = 90; C = 9×10×6 = 540. Rank by RPN: C, A, B. Severity of B, C is 9 or 10, so it needs specific attention regardless of RPN.

2.1.4-3.text: Three failure modes are rated as: Mode A: S 9, O 5, D 5; Mode B: S 10, O 9, D 9; Mode C: S 4, O 2, D 10. Compute each RPN and rank them. Is there any mode that needs attention regardless of its RPN?
2.1.4-3.answer: A = 9×5×5 = 225; B = 10×9×9 = 810; C = 4×2×10 = 80. Rank by RPN: B, A, C. Severity of A, B is 9 or 10, so it needs specific attention regardless of RPN.

2.1.4-4.text: Three failure modes are rated as: Mode A: S 6, O 4, D 6; Mode B: S 10, O 3, D 2; Mode C: S 2, O 2, D 2. Compute each RPN and rank them. Is there any mode that needs attention regardless of its RPN?
2.1.4-4.answer: A = 6×4×6 = 144; B = 10×3×2 = 60; C = 2×2×2 = 8. Rank by RPN: A, B, C. Severity of B is 9 or 10, so it needs specific attention regardless of RPN.

2.1.4-5.text: Three failure modes are rated as: Mode A: S 9, O 10, D 1; Mode B: S 8, O 8, D 9; Mode C: S 9, O 7, D 7. Compute each RPN and rank them. Is there any mode that needs attention regardless of its RPN?
2.1.4-5.answer: A = 9×10×1 = 90; B = 8×8×9 = 576; C = 9×7×7 = 441. Rank by RPN: B, C, A. Severity of A, C is 9 or 10, so it needs specific attention regardless of RPN.

2.1.4-6.text: Three failure modes are rated as: Mode A: S 2, O 4, D 1; Mode B: S 1, O 7, D 1; Mode C: S 4, O 5, D 10. Compute each RPN and rank them. Is there any mode that needs attention regardless of its RPN?
